text: You already know Docker containers exist — this course assumes that. What it doesn't assume is that you know what a Docker image actually is on disk: not one file, but a stack of immutable layers, merged at runtime by a union filesystem. That mechanism is why image pulls are fast, why disk usage is lower than you'd expect, and why Dockerfile instruction order is about to become a performance decision, not just a style choice.

Pull an image and Docker doesn't download one blob — it downloads several, each one a separately hashed layer. That hash is a SHA-256 digest of the layer's own content, so two images sharing a base layer only store it once; that's the 'already exists' line you'll see on a second pull. docker history shows this stack for any image already on disk, in the exact order the Dockerfile instructions that built it ran — metadata-only instructions like CMD and ENV show zero bytes, because they never touch the filesystem at all.

None of those layers get unpacked into one combined folder. The overlay2 storage driver — Docker's default on modern Linux — uses the kernel's own overlayfs to stack every read-only image layer and present one merged view to anything running inside. Only once you run the image does Docker add one more layer on top: a thin, container-specific writable layer, where every file change during that container's life actually lands, while the image layers underneath stay exactly as they were.

docker inspect's GraphDriver field makes this concrete: LowerDir lists the colon-separated, read-only image layers; UpperDir is the one layer unique to this specific running container. Modify a file that lives in a lower layer, and overlay2 copies it up into UpperDir before applying the change — classic copy-on-write — which is also why deleting a file in a later instruction never shrinks the image: the original bytes are still sitting in a lower layer, just hidden behind a whiteout marker.

That's the model: cached, content-addressed, cumulative layers underneath, one disposable writable layer on top per container. Next lesson puts it to direct use — because every RUN, COPY, and ADD in a Dockerfile produces exactly one of these layers, the order you write them in directly controls how much of your build cache survives from one build to the next, and how small the final image actually ends up.
